meta.title: Pulumi vs AWS: Which one to choose in 2026? (deployment, scaling & costs & code compared)
meta.description: Compare Pulumi and AWS architectural trade-offs, deployment, scaling, and infrastructure, and review side-by-side TypeScript to choose the right stack.

verdict: Choose Pulumi if you want a general-purpose infrastructure-as-code tool that uses mainstream programming languages and can manage AWS alongside other clouds and providers. Choose AWS-native tooling if you prefer a tightly integrated, AWS-supported platform and want to stay within one ecosystem. Many teams reasonably combine Pulumi for orchestration with native AWS services and IaC options.

comparison.toolA: Pulumi is an infrastructure-as-code platform that lets teams define and manage cloud resources using general-purpose languages such as TypeScript, Python, Go, and .NET, as well as YAML and templates. It is multi-cloud by design and can manage AWS resources through a dedicated provider alongside many other providers in the same program.
comparison.toolB: AWS is a cloud platform offering compute, storage, networking, databases, and many managed services, not a single IaC product. Its native infrastructure management options include CloudFormation, the AWS CDK, and other services, which are built specifically for AWS resources and integrate with AWS consoles, IAM, and deployment pipelines.

comparison.toolA: Pulumi's primary advantage is that engineers can use familiar programming languages, enabling loops, conditionals, functions, and existing testing and packaging tools. This can reduce the learning curve for teams already comfortable with TypeScript, Python, or Go, though it requires discipline to keep infrastructure code readable and well-structured.
comparison.toolB: AWS infrastructure-as-code options vary: CloudFormation uses JSON or YAML templates, while the AWS CDK supports TypeScript, Python, Java, C#, and Go and synthesizes to CloudFormation. Teams that prefer declarative templates may favor CloudFormation, while application developers often find the CDK more approachable.

comparison.toolA: Pulumi is designed to manage resources across multiple clouds and services from a single program, with providers for AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, and many SaaS platforms. This makes it attractive for organizations that need consistent workflows across heterogeneous environments, although provider maturity and feature coverage can differ by provider and version.
comparison.toolB: AWS-native tooling is optimized for AWS and generally tracks new AWS features quickly, but it is not intended to manage non-AWS resources as a primary use case. Organizations that are committed to AWS can benefit from this focus, while multi-cloud strategies typically require additional tools.

comparison.toolA: Pulumi integrates with common CI/CD systems, source control, and policy frameworks, and offers a managed cloud service as well as self-hosted options depending on plan and configuration. Because it is a third-party tool relative to AWS, integration depth and support arrangements depend on the Pulumi offerings and the team's setup.
comparison.toolB: AWS-native services are tightly integrated with IAM, CloudWatch, CloudTrail, and AWS Support plans, and AWS provides documentation and support for its own IaC options. Teams already standardized on AWS often value this native integration and the ability to get assistance directly from AWS, subject to the support plan purchased.

comparison.toolA: Pulumi maintains state for managed resources and offers a managed backend through Pulumi Cloud as well as self-managed backends, with features such as stack references and policy as code depending on plan. Operational complexity depends on whether teams use the managed service or self-host, and on how they configure secrets and concurrency controls.
comparison.toolB: CloudFormation manages stacks and state as a native AWS service, with drift detection, change sets, and rollback behavior built in, though limits and quotas apply. The AWS CDK synthesizes CloudFormation templates, so operations inherit CloudFormation's model, which can be simpler for AWS-only teams but less flexible outside AWS.

comparison.toolA: Pulumi can feel familiar to developers because it uses standard languages, but effective use still requires understanding cloud resources, state, and IaC concepts. Teams without strong software engineering practices may find the flexibility of general-purpose languages harder to govern than constrained templates.
comparison.toolB: CloudFormation templates are declarative and AWS-specific, which can be straightforward for simple stacks but verbose for complex ones. The AWS CDK lowers the barrier for developers but adds a synthesis step and its own constructs and conventions, so the best fit depends on team skills and existing AWS knowledge.

comparison.toolA: Pulumi supports policy as code and secrets management features that vary by plan and configuration, and it can apply consistent controls across providers. Security outcomes depend heavily on how state backends, credentials, and policies are configured, so teams should review the current documentation for their chosen plan.
comparison.toolB: AWS provides extensive native security and governance services such as IAM, Organizations, CloudTrail, Config, and Service Control Policies, and its IaC tools integrate with these services. Compliance features depend on the specific services and regions used, and teams should verify current certifications and regional availability for their requirements.

comparison.toolA: Pulumi offers a free tier and paid plans, with pricing that depends on features, users, and whether the managed service or self-hosted deployment is used. Exact costs should be confirmed against current Pulumi pricing, since plans and limits can change.
comparison.toolB: AWS charges for the cloud resources consumed, and its native IaC services such as CloudFormation generally do not carry a separate charge, though underlying resources and some related services do. Actual AWS costs vary widely by workload, region, and configuration, so estimates should be based on current AWS pricing.

faq.q: Is Pulumi an alternative to AWS?
faq.a: No. Pulumi is an infrastructure-as-code tool, while AWS is a cloud platform that provides the actual compute, storage, and managed services. Pulumi can manage AWS resources, so the two are often used together rather than as substitutes.

faq.q: Should I use Pulumi or AWS CloudFormation for AWS infrastructure?
faq.a: Pulumi is a strong fit if your team prefers general-purpose languages and wants to manage AWS alongside other providers. CloudFormation is a reasonable choice if you want an AWS-native, declarative service with tight integration into the AWS ecosystem. Evaluate based on team skills, multi-cloud needs, and governance requirements.

faq.q: Does Pulumi support all AWS services?
faq.a: Pulumi's AWS provider aims to cover AWS services, but feature coverage and timing can lag behind the newest AWS releases and may vary by provider version. Teams should verify support for the specific services and features they depend on before standardizing.

faq.q: Is the AWS CDK the same as Pulumi?
faq.a: They are similar in letting developers use programming languages to define infrastructure, but the AWS CDK synthesizes to CloudFormation and targets AWS, while Pulumi manages resources through its own engine and supports many providers. The right choice depends on whether you value AWS-native integration or provider flexibility.

faq.q: Which option is better for multi-cloud infrastructure?
faq.a: Pulumi is generally better suited to multi-cloud scenarios because it is designed to manage resources across many providers in a single workflow. AWS-native tooling is optimized for AWS, so multi-cloud use typically requires additional tools or processes.

faq.q: How do Pulumi and AWS handle security and compliance?
faq.a: AWS offers a broad set of native security and governance services that integrate with its IaC options, while Pulumi provides policy as code and secrets features that depend on plan and configuration. Both can be secure when configured carefully, and teams should verify current features and compliance details for their specific requirements.

faq.q: What should a small team choose in 2026?
faq.a: A small team already invested in AWS may find AWS-native IaC simpler to adopt and support, especially with the CDK or CloudFormation. A team with strong software engineering skills and multi-cloud or multi-provider needs may get more value from Pulumi, provided it can manage the operational overhead.

faq.q: Can I use Pulumi and AWS-native tools together?
faq.a: Yes, many organizations use Pulumi for orchestration while relying on AWS services and native tooling for specific workloads or teams. Mixing tools adds complexity, so define clear ownership, state management, and deployment boundaries to avoid conflicts.
